title: How To Increase Maturity And Independence Tenfold
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues today's students have less unstructured freedom than previous generations, resulting in rising immaturity and dependency, and that constant adult guidance and micromanagement have weakened students' internal self-starter capacity. His proposed remedy is simple but demanding: whenever students are doing what's expected, the teacher should fade into the background entirely—no praise, no narrating, no reminders, no acknowledgment—letting them fully own their success. This requires clear prior instruction and checked understanding, after which the teacher should become nearly invisible, allowing students to forget the teacher is even present. He argues this uninterrupted ownership of success, applied consistently across routines, lessons, and free play, builds a powerful sense of competence, autonomy, and motivation that separates a class from typical peers. The piece closes with a set of short phrases embodying the philosophy: 'This is what is expected,' 'You can do this,' 'You don't need me,' 'I believe in you.'
points: Today's students are said to have less unstructured freedom than past generations, contributing to rising immaturity and dependency.
Excessive adult guidance and micromanagement are identified as weakening students' internal self-starter capacity and ability to play independently.
The core strategy: once students are doing what's expected, the teacher should disappear entirely—no praise, narrating, reminders, or acknowledgment.
This approach requires clear prior instruction and a checked understanding before students are released to work.
Consistently applying this hands-off approach across routines, lessons, and free play is claimed to build competence, autonomy, and motivation 'tenfold.'
quotes: Right or wrong, today’s students have less freedom than in decades past. Generally speaking, their lives are more controlled, organized, and edited.

All the guiding, advising, directing, and micromanaging very effectively weakens our students’ internal self-starter mechanism. It paralyzes their imagination, creativity, and ability to visualize, set, and attain their own goals.

It is this: Whenever your students are doing what you want, asked of them, or expected—no matter what it is— leave them alone . As much as possible, you want to disappear, become a fly on the wall, and just observe .

The moment they begin giving you what you want, don’t step in to praise or encourage. Don’t narrate, remind, or rehash. Don’t kneel down and ask questions or offer hints and clues. Don’t even acknowledge.

The idea is for them to forget that you’re even there, to rely on themselves and their classmates, and to carry the full weight of responsibility—which feels good and empowers them with the ability to know how to learn and succeed no matter the obstacles.
